newsitem.title: UK: UK to scrap all anti-personnel landmines by 2005.
newsitem.headline: UK to scrap all anti-personnel landmines by 2005.

text.p: The new Labour government promised on Wednesday to destroy all Britain's anti-personnel landmines by 2005, pursuing its pledge to put human rights at the centre of foreign policy.
The previous Conservative government had also vowed to scrap its stocks of so-called APLs but gave no target date.
It had also reserved the right to replace the weapons with "smart mines", which self-detonate after a certain period, but the new government said it would shun these replacements.
"We are going to ban any export, import, transfer of landmines from Britain," Foreign Secretary Robin Cook told CCN news in an interview.
"There will be no British part played anywhere in the trade in landmines...and we have also announced that they will not be used with British troops," he added.
Prime Minister Tony Blair told parliament that mines have done enormous carnage and banning them was "the right and civilised thing to do."
Since taking power this month, Labour has stressed the need for action on landmines, blamed for killing 25,000 people a year and maiming many more.
The Red Cross estimates there are 120 million mines in the ground across the world, many of them in poor war-torn countries such as Angola and Cambodia.

Although the government will ban the import, export and manufacture of APLs in reality this does not represent much of a policy change since Britain has not bought, sold or built the weapons for several years.
Analysts say the shift on smart mines is more significant since it rules out any backsliding.
"The prospect of obtaining new smart mines has now disappeared," a defence official told reporters after Cook announced the policy change in a statement.
Cook said Britain would scrap all APLs by 2005 and in the meanwhile would observe a moratorium on their use until 2005 or until an effective international ban was introduced.
Despite the determination to abolish APLs, Cook said the armed forces retained the right to use them and that parliament would only be informed after the fact.
"We have said that in very exceptional circumstances we may give ministerial authority for the use of landmines in exceptional cases. We don't want to do that," Cook said.
The British Red Cross and the UK Working Group on Landmines welcomed the initiative which they said could help achieve a global ban on anti-personnel landmines.

"The speed at which the new government has moved mirrors the urgency of the issue. It has been triggered by the public's overwhelming call for a ban," said Tim Carstairs of the UK Working Group on Landmines, a grouping of some 50 British agencies including Oxfam, Christian Aid and World Vision.

British officials said the government also intended to sign up to the so-called Ottawa Process, a Canadian initiative grouping 50 nations which want to sign a treaty by the end of this year to ban the production, stockpiling, export and use of mines.

The United States declared last week that it would not join the Canadian pact, saying the only forum where a universal ban could be worked out was the U.N.'s separate Geneva-based Conference on Disarmament.
